To determine which module should be used for inference, the CU compares the summation of the last four anomaly scores from RM against the corre- sponding summation from SM. By default, RM is preferred due to its speed advantage, but if its accumulated anomaly score is higher than SM’s, the CU shifts reliance to SM for better accuracy. A shorter window (e.g., one or two scores) may lead to erratic switching between RM and SM, while a longer window (e.g., ten or more) could result in slow adaptation to changing patterns. Both RM and SM receive the same input in parallel, ensuring that inference remains synchronized. This mechanism allows RMtobeleveragedforfastpredictionswhilemaintainingtherobustnessofSM for more challenging cases. During training, the CU follows these memory update rules: • RM Incorrect, SM Incorrect: – Both RM and SM update their predictions. – RM’s recurrence counts are adjusted to improve future predictions. • RM Incorrect, SM Correct: – SM’s output is used, bypassing RM. – RM reduces its recurrence count for the incorrect prediction. 15 – RM is retrained to align with SM’s accurate predictions. • RM Correct, SM Incorrect: – RM’s prediction is used, bypassing SM. – SM is trained with a regular confidence update to improve accuracy. • RM Correct, SM Correct: – RM’s output is used to expedite response time. – SM is reinforced with a higher confidence update. However, its computational overhead, par- ticularly in SM, has led to various acceleration techniques, including hardware implementations and software optimizations. Hardware-based methods typi- callyleverageparallelcomputationandspecializedmemoryarchitectures,while software optimizations focus on reducing computational complexity or improv- ing learning mechanisms. Several hardware accelerators have been proposed for HTM. FPGA-based implementations achieve 3× speedups through parallelism but consume high power [38]. Memristor-based architectures enhance efficiency with non-volatile memory but face reliability issues [39]. Neuromorphic computing, inspired by biologicallearning,acceleratesHTMbutrequiresspecializedhardware,limiting generalizability [40]. Activation intensity-based learning cut training time by 29%–61% through adaptive learning rates [42]. A GRU-enhanced HTM improved long-term prediction but increased training time by 22%–105%, raising computational costs [43]. Our approach introduces two key innovations that distinguish it from prior works. First, AHTM, incorporating RM, specializes in first-order inference, inspired by biological reflex arcs. Unlike previous HTM accelerations that fo- cus on optimizing full-sequence learning, AHTM efficiently offloads repetitive patterns, reducing computational overhead while maintaining accuracy. JSON: Name: reflex_memory_ahtm Title: Accelerating hierarchical temporal memory inference for streaming financial anomaly detection using a reflex memory module and CAM-based hardware augmentation Short Hypothesis: Adding a fixed-size, frequency-indexed Reflex Memory (RM) module with a control unit that preferentially routes first-order predictions to RM will reduce average inference latency on streaming financial time-series by at least 5× compared to standard HTM sequence memory while keeping anomaly detection F1 score within 5% of the HTM baseline. Related Work: Existing approaches to accelerating Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) split into three categories: software parallelization, neuromorphic/specialized hardware, and memory/search-optimized hardware. Software/GPU parallelization achieves large kernel speedups but preserves high overall latency and memory traffic. FPGA and neuromorphic implementations reduce latency via parallelism or specialized neuron models but require high power budgets or bespoke platforms and often trade generality for speed. Emerging non-volatile memory and memristor proposals reduce storage and enable in-memory operations but face endurance, variability, and mapping challenges. Prior work has not combined a biologically inspired, fixed-size first-order cache with a selective attention control mechanism, nor mapped such a cache directly to a content-addressable memory (CAM) primitive for sub-millisecond prediction. Limitations across prior methods include: persistent high computational cost for first-order repetitive transitions, lack of a principled module to offload frequent patterns, dependence on specialized hardware that limits deployability, and insufficient evaluation of accuracy vs. latency trade-offs in online streaming settings. Abstract: Streaming sensors and financial feeds require low-latency unsupervised inference for anomaly detection, but Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) sequence memory (SM) incurs computational overhead when processing frequently recurring first-order transitions. We propose an accelerated HTM pipeline that integrates a Reflex Memory (RM) — a fixed-size, frequency-indexed dictionary for first-order transitions — and a Control Unit (CU) that routes predictions to RM or SM based on recent confidence. For hardware acceleration, RM is mapped onto a content-addressable memory (CAM) microarchitecture to enable sub-millisecond associative lookup and ranking by frequency. The principal contribution is a hybrid online-learning pipeline that (1) offloads high-frequency first-order inference to RM to reduce latency, (2) preserves multi-order sequence learning in SM, and (3) provides a CAM-aware RM implementation for further acceleration. We expect the pipeline to deliver multi-fold inference speedups on streaming financial time-series while maintaining comparable anomaly-detection accuracy to baseline HTM, enabling real-time detection and continuous adaptation without full retraining. Experiments: Datasets: Dow Jones (weekly, 2,082 points), NASDAQ (weekly, 2,083), S&P 500 (weekly, 2,084), Gold Prices (monthly, 842), S&P 500 extended (monthly, 1,766, multiple financial features), VIX variants (daily and monthly, ~4,053), Natural Gas (daily, 5,802), Oil Prices (daily, 8,303). Preprocessing: normalize numeric series, apply identical encoder to produce 1,024-bit SDRs. Baselines: (A) HTM with standard Sequence Memory (SM), (B) AHTM: HTM + software RM (no CAM), (C) GPU/OpenCL-accelerated HTM kernel, (D) LSTM/GRU anomaly detector trained in online mode. Proposed variants: (P1) AHTM with CU window = {1,4,8,16}, (P2) H-AHTM: AHTM with CAM-backed RM. Evaluation metrics: anomaly detection precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC; per-sample inference latency (mean, 95th percentile); throughput (samples/s); memory footprint (MB); energy-per-prediction (nJ) for hardware-modeled H-AHTM; online adaptation measured as change in F1 after injecting 10% novel pattern drift. Experimental setup: software experiments run on an 8-core Intel i9, 3.0 GHz, 10 GB RAM, Linux; repeat each trial 10 times and report mean ± std. Hardware-modeled evaluation: use FeFET-based CAM SPICE model (14 nm equivalent) and synthesized register/decoder blocks to estimate latency and energy per operation. Ablations: (i) remove CU (always use RM when present) vs CU-enabled; (ii) vary RM capacity {512,1024,2048,4096} entries to measure latency vs accuracy; (iii) compare software RM vs CAM-backed RM keeping algorithmic parameters identical. Statistical analysis: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test for latency and F1 differences (α=0.05). Success criteria: demonstration of ≥5× median inference latency reduction of P2 over baseline HTM with F1 degradation ≤5%. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) RM eviction and fixed-size constraints: finite RM capacity can evict moderately frequent but semantically important transitions, causing increased false negatives or catastrophic forgetting. 2) Accuracy-speed trade-off: preferential routing to RM risks lower accuracy on sequences requiring multi-order context; CU tuning may be sensitive to workload. 3) CAM hardware reliability and endurance: FeFET/novel CAM cells have write endurance, retention, and variability limitations that affect long-term correctness and energy estimates. 4) Mapping fidelity: SPICE and synthesized estimates may not capture full-system integration costs (interconnect, controller overhead), leading to optimistic latency/energy numbers. 5) Dataset bias and domain transfer: experiments on financial time-series may not generalize to other modalities with different temporal statistics; performance may degrade on non-redundant streams. 6) Hyperparameter sensitivity: SDR size, RM size, CU window, and thresholds require tuning; results may be brittle across datasets. 7) Adversarial and corner-case sequences: deliberately engineered inputs might trigger repeated misrouting to RM, increasing error. 8) Scalability: as SDR dimensionality or required RM capacity grows, CAM area and power scale unfavorably; system may not fit edge device constraints. 9) Evaluation limitations: hardware-in-the-loop validation absent; simulated hardware metrics cannot substitute for silicon measurements.
